newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton, Jiang break the ice at APEC summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Jiang break the ice at APEC summit.

text.p: With warm handshakes and broad smiles, U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Sunday broke the ice on Sino-U.S. ties.
Analysts said their cordial meeting, in which they swapped invitations for summits in each other's capitals, indicated that relations were bouncing back after a crisis in the Taiwan Strait in March.
"It is a marked improvement over the low point in Sino-American relations around the time of the Taiwanese presidential elections earlier this year," said Geremie Barme, a leading China scholar.
"The Chinese to have engaged positively with the Americans in this type of public meeting between presidents is significant."

Relations reached a critical point when China conducted missile tests as Taiwan held its first free elections for the presidency. The United States sent two aircraft carrier battle groups to the area in response.
Sunday's agreement did more than just put China and the United States on friendly speaking terms again.
Some saw it as a sunny omen for the much-heralded "Pacific Century", which many believe will be dominated by vibrant economies represented at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Manila.

In a booming region that is home to two billion people, accounts for 40 percent of global trade and more than a half of the world's economic output, no relationship is more vital than the one between China and the United States.
And for almost a decade that relationship has been deeply troubled.

Sino-U.S. disputes over human rights, Taiwan, arms proliferation, intellectual property rights and market opening have cast a dark shadow over regional security and trade flows around the Pacific Rim.

"A stable U.S.-China relationship will mean stability and growth. An ad hoc and spasmodic relationship will cause uncertainty and instability, and inhibit growth throughout East Asia," Singapore's senior minister Lee Kuan Yew said recently.
China, once Asia's sleeping giant, is now wide awake and restless.
For many, the question is whether its inexorable rise as an economic superpower will be peaceful or accompanied by a clash of civilisations across the Pacific.

Asia-Pacific nations forging a free trade zone among themselves hope that by easing smoothly into a regional partnership with the United States, China will have too great a stake in the area's prosperty to risk political or military adventure.

"It is in everyone's interests that China should be given every incentive to choose international cooperation which will absorb its energies constructively for another 50 to 100 years," Lee said in his speech.
"If such a route is not open to China, the world must live with a pushy China."

Washington and Beijing have been at loggerheads since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre exposed their deep differences. The last U.S. president to visit Beijing was George Bush shortly before the student democracy movement was crushed by guns and tanks.
A modernising China challenged not only U.S. ecomomic supremacy but also its most cherished values.
Hawks in the United States saw signs that Beijing wanted eventually to confront the world's only superpower through force of arms as well, and called for a policy of "containment".
Amid rising nationalism in China, the Beijing leadership accused Washington of trying to stunt its economic rise. It dug in its heels over trade issues and human rights.
"The Chinese have been talking about an unofficial strategy on the part of the Americans to encircle China, to contain China," said Barme. "Whether that is the case or not is highly questionable."
Asian leaders welcomed warming U.S. ties with China.
"I am very happy that the U.S.-China summit was conducted in a good atmosphere," a senior Japanese official quoted Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto as telling Clinton.
"It is not advisable to seek the isolation of China, and China is our important partner in this region," Hashimoto said. "I am happy that things are moving in the correct direction."
